newsitem.title: INDIA: India says broadcast law likely by year-end.
newsitem.headline: India says broadcast law likely by year-end.

text.p: India said on Wednesday that a bill seeking to allow private broadcasters to beam radio and television programmes from the country was likely to be approved by parliament late this year.

"I am reasonably confident that we will be able to adopt the bill in the winter session of parliament," Information and Broadcasting Minister Jaipal Reddy told a seminar on the planned broadcast law in the Indian capital.
The month-long winter session starts in November.
"We are hopeful the bill would come into effect by early next year," Reddy added.
The Broadcast Bill, a tentative draft of which was introduced in parliament in May, is being examined by a multi-party committee of lawmakers.
They are expected to suggest changes in the bill, which seeks to end decades of state monopoly over the airwaves.
State-run All India Radio (AIR) and Doordarshan television currently rent out time slots to private broadcasters, but private broadcasting stations are not allowed.

The bill has irked foreign firms because in its present form, it limits their stakes in satellite broadcast companies to 49 percent and totally bars foreign equity in private firms bidding for terrestrial, or local, broadcasting licences.
Industry officials urged the government to ease some of the restrictions proposed in the bill.

"The 49 percent cap on foreign equity participation proposed in the Broadcast Bill has caused an acrimonious debate," a statement issued by the Associated Chambers of Commerce and Industry of India (ASSOCHAM) said.
ASSOCHAM, which organised the seminar, said it was unrealistic to force satellite broadcasters currently beaming their programmes from outside into India to uplink from India.
Om Wadhwa, an expert appointed by ASSOCHAM, said all satellite broadcasters currently beaming into the country were foreign firms with 100 percent equity stakes.
"Whether we have enough resources to ask foreign firms to divest has to be first examined," Wadhwa said.
Wadhwa also urged the minister to increase the validity of the proposed licence period for private broadcasters to at least 15 years from the proposed 10 years.
A proposal by Rupert Murdoch's Star Television, a unit of News Corp, to launch direct-to-home (DTH) satellite broadcasting in India has run into trouble following a recent ban by the government.
DTH services require small dish antennae at the customer's end. Government officials say the services cannot start until the parliament approves the Broadcast Bill.
Reddy said the government was not opposed to DTH services but added they should be subject to regulation. "Therefore we first need the regulatory authority," he said.
